clue.text: You rarely now having the energy

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so the letters are contained in the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A complaint that people seldom seem to have any get-up-and-go these days.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads like a grumble about modern listlessness, but it describes an archaic word: THEE is the old form of 'you', rarely used now. The whole of 'the' plus the first letter of 'energy' spell it.
explanation.definitionFit: Thee is the archaic object form of the second-person pronoun, surviving mainly in prayers, dialect and old poetry.

clue.text: Friendly message written by French chum

indicators.note: something written by a person sits beside their name, so one piece follows the other

parts.note: ami is French for friend
a cable is a telegram

explanation.surface: A warm note penned by a pal from France.
explanation.walkthrough: The message comes first in the clue but the French friend comes first in the answer; 'written by' lets the chum sign ahead of the cable.
explanation.definitionFit: Amicable describes relations that are good-natured and without hostility, a close synonym for friendly.

clue.text: Test is ordeal with a couple dropping out

indicators.note: whatever drops out leaves the group, so letters are removed

parts.note: taken as written
a couple is two, here two neighbouring letters of the word

explanation.surface: An exam described as a trial that a pair of candidates quit.
explanation.walkthrough: The couple dropping out sounds like two examinees giving up; it is two letters, D and E, leaving the middle of ORDEAL to give ORAL.
explanation.definitionFit: An oral is a spoken examination, as in a language exam or a viva, so it is a kind of test.

clue.text: A body-builder for a heavenly body

parts.note: taken as written
anabolic steroids are drugs taken to build muscle

explanation.surface: A gym-goer's drug promising a divine physique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavenly body' plays on the gym sense of a perfect physique, but it is an object in space. A body-builder here is what builds a body: a steroid.
explanation.definitionFit: An asteroid is a small rocky object orbiting the sun, one of the celestial objects astronomers call heavenly bodies.

clue.text: Computer container chum knocked over

indicators.note: something knocked over ends up upside down, so in a down clue the letters run the other way

parts.note: a pot is a container
a pal is a chum

explanation.surface: A friend clumsily knocks a computer case to the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole charade POT + PAL is turned over at once, so both parts are reversed and swap places.
explanation.definitionFit: A laptop is a portable personal computer designed to rest on the user's knees.

clue.text: Our customers perhaps shocked by her despair

indicators.note: something shocked is jolted out of its settled state, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A business's customers are dismayed by a woman's hopelessness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our customers perhaps' is spoken by a newspaper: for a publication, its customers are its readers. 'Perhaps' flags that this is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper or magazine's readership is the body of people who buy and read it, its customers in effect.

clue.text: Pair in church with one of the royals

parts.note: PR is the standard abbreviation for pair
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A couple at a church wedding alongside a member of the royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it puts the pair inside the church, but it is simply taken as the letters IN between the two abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A prince is a son or grandson of a monarch, a male member of a royal family.

clue.text: Military supplies needed by team momentarily

indicators.note: what is needed by something is held within it, so the letters sit inside the following words

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A squad briefly requires provisions for the army.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts in the last two letters of 'team' and finishes at the start of 'momentarily'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammo is the informal short form of ammunition, the bullets and shells an army is supplied with.

clue.text: Poet in dwelling by river

indicators.note: one thing standing by another is next to it, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: a home is a dwelling
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A writer living in a riverside cottage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' seems to place the poet inside the house, but it only joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer is the ancient Greek bard credited with the epic poems the Iliad and the Odyssey.

clue.text: Captured unusual percussion instrument

parts.note: to snare an animal is to capture it
rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: Someone has seized a strange instrument from the orchestra's back row.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' looks like it describes the instrument, but it is the old British word 'rum', meaning peculiar.
explanation.definitionFit: A snare drum is a shallow drum with wires stretched across its underside, a staple of bands and drum kits.

clue.text: Smashing old room at front of hospital department

indicators.note: being at the front of something means coming just before it, fixing the order of the pieces

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
a cell is a small room, as in a monastery or prison
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: A wrecked former ward standing at the entrance to a hospital unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' suggests destruction, fitting the hospital scene, but it is British slang for wonderful.
explanation.definitionFit: Smashing is informal British praise meaning outstandingly good, the same sense as first-rate or superb.

clue.text: Put wild dog in here

indicators.note: something wild is unruly and out of control, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
part of the instruction to the solver, giving no letters
the grid square the solver is writing in, giving no letters

explanation.surface: An instruction to lock a feral hound up in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is an instruction to the solver: write a wild dog in the grid here, and a wild arrangement of 'dog in' is exactly that animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The dingo is the untamed canine native to Australia, descended from domestic dogs but living free.

clue.text: Odd taboo about cocaine, repeatedly seen as harmful product

indicators.note: about means around, so one set of letters wraps round another
something odd is out of the ordinary, so the letters leave their usual order

parts.note: taken as written
C is slang for cocaine, and 'repeatedly' doubles it

explanation.surface: A strange ban on drugs being used again and again, the stuff regarded as damaging.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged taboo is split after its fourth letter so the two Cs sit inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tobacco is a plant product smoked or chewed for its nicotine, notorious for causing cancer and heart disease.

clue.text: One must be involved in diplomacy — that is understood

indicators.note: to be involved in something is to be caught up inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: tact is skill in handling people delicately
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A reminder that diplomatic work requires participation, which goes without saying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' looks like it opens an explanation, but it is only the link to the definition at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit describes something implied or accepted without being stated aloud, as in a tacit agreement.

clue.text: HQ penetrated by the enemy unit

indicators.note: whatever is penetrated has something forced into it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a centre is a headquarters, the hub of operations
from the saying 'time is the enemy'

explanation.surface: A military unit whose headquarters has been infiltrated by hostile forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unit' seems to be a military one in this war story, but it is a unit of measurement. 'Time is the enemy' is the familiar saying behind the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A centimetre is a hundredth of a metre, a standard metric measure of length.

clue.text: Signal in harbour to finish

parts.note: a port is a harbour
an end is a finish

explanation.surface: A lamp flashes in the harbour to mark the end of the day's sailing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Signal' looks like a noun for a lighthouse flash, but it is a verb meaning to foreshadow.
explanation.definitionFit: To portend is to be an omen or warning of something to come, which is to signal it in advance.

clue.text: Road flooded by broad river

indicators.note: something flooded by water is submerged inside it, so the letters lie within the next words

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A street under water after a wide river burst its banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River' suggests the abbreviation R, but here the whole word is part of the concealed run.
explanation.definitionFit: Drive is used in street names for a road, and also for a private road leading up to a house.

clue.text: Charlie, thin and hygienic

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
lean means thin

explanation.surface: A description of a man called Charlie as slim and spotless.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie looks like a person's name, but it is the radio code word for the letter C.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hygienic is free from dirt and germs, which is what being clean means.

clue.text: Expert seen as wicked on reflection

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things back to front, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: bad means wicked

explanation.surface: A specialist who, after some thought, comes across as evil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On reflection' reads as 'after thinking it over', not as a mirror image.
explanation.definitionFit: A dab, or dab hand, is British informal for someone highly skilled at something.

clue.text: One in worship like a jellyfish

indicators.note: a thing placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: to bless is to praise or glorify, as in worship
taken as written

explanation.surface: A worshipper at a service who resembles a spineless sea creature.
explanation.walkthrough: The jellyfish image suggests softness or cowardice, but the definition is literal: a jellyfish has no skeleton.
explanation.definitionFit: Jellyfish have soft gelatinous bodies with no skeleton at all, so they have no bones.

clue.text: Attire bishop shed coming to one country

indicators.note: what is shed is cast off, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a habit is a monk's or nun's garment
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A bishop sheds his robes on arriving in a particular nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' sounds like undressing, fitting the attire, but it removes the letter B from the garment word.
explanation.definitionFit: Haiti is a Caribbean nation occupying the western part of the island of Hispaniola.

clue.text: One sister and one lad agreeing

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a nun is a religious sister
I is the Roman numeral one
a son is a lad, a boy

explanation.surface: A nun and a boy who see eye to eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sister' reads as a sibling, but in crosswords it often means a nun.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in unison is to act or speak together in complete harmony, sharing one view.

clue.text: A gent is terribly irritating

indicators.note: something done terribly is done badly, so the letters come out in a wrong order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint that a certain gentleman is extremely annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terribly' looks like an intensifier for 'irritating', but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Teasing, as an adjective, describes behaviour that provokes or annoys someone by mocking or tormenting them playfully.

clue.text: Upper-class type a riot's upset

indicators.note: something upset is overturned and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A posh person disturbed by an outbreak of civil unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as the aristocrat's feelings, but it tells you to shuffle the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristo is informal short for aristocrat, a member of the nobility or upper classes.

clue.text: Awful danger in Eden?

indicators.note: something awful is in a bad state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning about the serpent lurking in paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: Eden is one particular garden, the biblical one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Garden of Eden is the paradise of Genesis where Adam and Eve lived before the Fall.

clue.text: Write about air? Atmosphere is unbreathable on this planet

definitions.text: Atmosphere is unbreathable on this planet

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, as in about-turn, so the letters face the other way

parts.note: to pen is to write
an air is a melody

explanation.surface: A writer considers the air, noting that on some other world it could not be breathed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' fits the atmosphere theme, but it means a tune. The definition is a descriptive phrase: this gas giant's methane-rich atmosphere is poisonous.
explanation.definitionFit: Neptune is the eighth planet from the sun, a gas giant whose hydrogen, helium and methane envelope could not support human life.

clue.text: Lots of sheets, not all required

indicators.note: taking not all of a word means using only part of it

parts.note: the letters sit inside the word, dropping its first two and last

explanation.surface: Plenty of paper, though you won't need every page.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lots of sheets' sounds like bed linen, but it is a paper measure.
explanation.definitionFit: A quire is a traditional paper quantity of twenty-four or twenty-five leaves, one twentieth of a ream.

clue.text: Who in Calais needs boat finally to leave

parts.note: qui is French for who; Calais is a French port

indicators.note: finally points to the last in line, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone in the French port wants a ferry to get away.
explanation.walkthrough: Naming a French town is a crossword signal to translate into French.
explanation.definitionFit: To quit a place is to depart from it, the same as going away or leaving.

clue.text: Turning less colourful, Carol is declining in health

indicators.note: turning means rotating round, so the letters face the opposite way

parts.note: paler means having less colour
to carol is to sing joyfully

explanation.surface: A woman named Carol is losing her colour and her health is failing.
explanation.walkthrough: Carol looks like a woman's name, but it is the verb meaning to sing.
explanation.definitionFit: A patient who relapses falls back into illness after seeming to improve, so their health gets worse.

clue.text: At side of street dad is tense

indicators.note: being at the side of something means sitting next to it, so the pieces join end to end

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: A father standing on the pavement is feeling nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks like an adjective for anxious, but it is the grammar noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The past is the grammatical tense for actions already completed, as in 'walked'.

clue.text: Greta's short dress

indicators.note: cutting something short trims its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: Greta Garbo was the Swedish-born Hollywood film star

explanation.surface: A film star's frock that is rather brief.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive makes it sound like a dress belonging to Greta; it is her surname, Garbo, with its tail cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: Garb means clothing, especially distinctive attire, so it works as a synonym for dress as a noun.

clue.text: Prisoners chopping up nine trees

indicators.note: chopping up breaks things into pieces that can be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Convicts on a work detail felling a small stand of timber.
explanation.walkthrough: The picture of labouring prisoners makes 'chopping up' look literal; it tells you to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Internees are people confined, usually in wartime or for political reasons, without trial, so they are held captive.

clue.text: Son without much money on track

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son
being poor means having little money

explanation.surface: A penniless young man heads off down a path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Track' reads as a path or railway, but it means the trail an animal leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoor is the trail of footprints or droppings left by a wild animal, followed by hunters.
